body.text: For Canada's federal SR&ED program, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada—whether a corporation, individual, partnership member or trust beneficiary—that performs qualifying SR&ED in Canada is legally entitled to claim the incentives, provided it files Form T661 and the prescribed schedule within the statutory reporting deadline, earning investment tax credits at 15% or 35%.

This report provides a comprehensive legal, financial, and technical audit of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture of Canada as of November 2026. The primary authorities reviewed encompass the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), the Income Tax Regulations, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (Bill C-15, S.C. 2026, c. 3), official Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) policies and guidelines updated through October 2026, provincial and territorial tax statutes, and jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada, the Federal Court of Appeal, and the Supreme Court of Canada.

Industry estimates place annual distributions under Canada's flagship innovation incentive—the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—at more than $4.5 billion. Between December 2024 and March 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most substantial legislative expansion since 2012. Following initial proposals in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and further enhancements in Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025), Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the enacted legislation doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for depreciable property acquired or leased after December 15, 2024.

Concurrently, the provincial R&D landscape experienced major structural shifts across 2025 and 2026. In its 2025–2026 Budget (tabled March 25, 2025), Québec abolished eight legacy R&D tax credits and consolidated its innovation regime into the new fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, providing a 30% rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above a modified exclusion threshold and 20% on the excess. British Columbia made its 10% provincial SR&ED credit permanent in BC Budget 2026 and fully harmonized with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, $15 million–$75 million phase-out range, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration. Saskatchewan doubled its CCPC refundable credit threshold from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 and restored capital expenditure eligibility retroactive to December 16, 2024, while Ontario confirmed in its October 29, 2026 Fall Economic Statement that restored federal capital expenditures flow through to its provincial R&D credits while maintaining its $3,000,000 cap on the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC).

body.text: Section 1: Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 The Dual-Pillar Incentive Framework Under the Income Tax Act

Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive regime is codified in the Income Tax Act (ITA) and Section 2900 (and related provisions) of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Unlike competitive or discretionary government grants, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement: any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that performs qualifying SR&ED in Canada and files the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information within the statutory reporting deadline is legally entitled to claim the incentives. Under the Canadian tax system, the program operates through two distinct but interconnected statutory mechanisms:

items: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Section 37 of the ITA): Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may pool all allowable current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada. This pool allows full current deductibility or indefinite carryforward against business income.

The SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA): Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), taxpayers earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Under section 127.1, qualifying claimants may receive all or a portion of their unused ITCs as a direct cash refund.

body.text: 1.2 Mechanics of the Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool

The Section 37 pool operates as a cumulative, running balance tracked on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim). Because a positive balance in the pool does not expire, the CRA administers the pool as an aggregate running total and only identifies the total balance carried forward, without tracking or recording the specific taxation year to which each historical expenditure amount relates.
Additions to the Section 37(1) Pool
Pursuant to subsection 37(1) and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is increased each taxation year by six statutory categories:

First, the pool is increased by expenditures of a current nature incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(a). This encompasses SR&ED directly undertaken by the claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant under contract (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), third-party payments made to corporations resident in Canada (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)), third-party payments made to approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, non-profit SR&ED corporations, or granting councils (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)), and payments by a corporation to tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations for basic or applied research (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)). Specific current expenditure items added under paragraph 37(1)(a) include the eligible portion of salary or wages of employees, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (as well as historical pre-2014 lease costs), contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on the claimant's behalf, eligible third-party payments, and—only where the claimant elects the Traditional Method—directly attributable overhead expenditures.

Second, the pool is increased under paragraph 37(1)(b) by expenditures of a capital nature incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (as well as historical capital property acquired prior to 2014) that satisfies the "all or substantially all" (ASA ≥90%) intention test. Third, the pool is increased by repayments of government assistance or non-government assistance that had previously reduced the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; such repayments are treated as expenditures pursuant to the ITA. Fourth, the pool is increased by amounts included in income in a previous taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA (where a negative pool balance at the end of a prior taxation year was included in income and added back to reset the subsequent year's opening pool balance to nil). Fifth, the pool includes any balance of deductible SR&ED expenditures transferred on an amalgamation or wind-up. Sixth, the pool is increased by the amount of any SR&ED ITC recaptured in the prior taxation year (including amounts added due to partnership ITC recapture excess amounts).
Reductions to the Section 37(1) Pool
Conversely, the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is decreased under subsection 37(1) by five categories of reductions:

items: Government and Non-Government Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(d)): All amounts of government assistance or non-government assistance (including provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, except the portion relating to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount) that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive for SR&ED expenditures included in the pool.
Super-Allowance Benefit Amounts: Any "super-allowance benefit amount" for the year or for preceding taxation years in respect of a province.
Prior-Year Federal ITCs Claimed or Refunded (Paragraph 37(1)(e)): Federal SR&ED ITCs applied against Part I tax payable, carried back, or refunded in cash in a preceding taxation year.
Prior Pool Deductions (Paragraph 37(1)(f)): Amounts deducted from the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years.

Insolvency Deductions (Paragraph 37(1)(f.1)): Amounts deducted by the claimant with respect to insolvency under section 61.3 in preceding years, to the extent those amounts did not exceed the pool balance in the year claimed.

body.text: Indefinite Carryforward, Optionality, and Partnership Restrictions

A claimant (other than a partnership) has the option of deducting the entire available balance of the Section 37(1) pool in a taxation year or deducting only a portion (or none) and carrying forward the unclaimed positive balance indefinitely to deduct against business income in any subsequent taxation year. Deferring the Section 37(1) deduction allows a corporation to create or preserve taxable income in the current year so that it can utilize foreign tax credits or expiring investment tax credits. Furthermore, utilizing an existing balance from the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in a subsequent year is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, provided the underlying expenditures were identified on time on Form T661 for the year in which they were originally incurred.

By contrast, a partnership is not permitted to carry forward an amount in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period. Because partnership income is computed at the partnership level before flowing through to partners, the entire balance of the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be fully deducted in calculating the partnership's net income for tax purposes in that period.
Acquisition of Control / Loss Restriction Event (Subsections 37(6.1) and 37(1)(h))

When control of a corporation is acquired (a "loss restriction event"), a deemed taxation year-end occurs immediately before the acquisition of control, and the corporation's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1). Similarly, a trust's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil at the time there is a new majority-interest beneficiary. In a subsequent taxation year, the undeducted portion of the pool from before the loss restriction event may be reinstated, carried forward, and deducted in calculating income for tax purposes only if two cumulative statutory conditions are met:

items: The business to which the SR&ED expenditures related is continued for profit, or with a reasonable expectation of profit; and

The deduction is limited to the extent that the taxpayer's income for the subsequent taxation year (before making any deduction from the Section 37 pool) is derived from that same business or from a similar business.

body.text: Research Carried On Outside Canada (Subsection 37(2))

Expenditures of a current nature incurred by a taxpayer in carrying on SR&ED outside Canada are governed separately by subsection 37(2) of the ITA. While current expenditures for foreign research may be deducted in computing net business income or loss in the year incurred under subsection 37(2), they cannot be included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, cannot be claimed on Form T661, and do not earn any Investment Tax Credit. The sole statutory exception is for "permissible salary or wages" paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), which may be included in the subsection 37(1) pool up to a 10% cap.
1.3 Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" is housed in subsection 248(1) of the ITA (having replaced former Regulation 2900(1)). Evaluating whether work is eligible requires verifying the work against the preamble, the four inclusive paragraphs ((a) through (d)), and the seven explicit exclusions ((e) through (k)) of subsection 248(1).
The Preamble and Core Categories (Paragraphs 248(1)(a) to (c))

Under the preamble to subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of three core categories:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The majority of private-sector SR&ED claims in Canada focus on experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c). The statutory phrase "including incremental improvements thereto" confirms that an evolutionary improvement to an existing material, device, product, or process qualifies, provided the work seeks to achieve a technological advancement by resolving a technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved through standard practice or routine engineering.

body.text: Directly Supporting Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d))

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), SR&ED also includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive categories: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, and (8) psychological research.

However, work in these eight categories is eligible only where the work is "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work by itself does not meet the legal definition of SR&ED. Moreover, "commensurate with the needs" restricts eligible support work to the scope strictly required to support the experimental investigation; once the technological uncertainty is resolved, routine engineering, design, or coding for commercial production ceases to qualify.
The Seven Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))
Subsection 248(1) expressly excludes any work with respect to seven enumerated activities ("the exclusions"), which cannot be claimed under any circumstances:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes;
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas;
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes; and
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection.

body.text: Under the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, the key feature that distinguishes eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) (such as data collection or testing) from excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of performing basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it qualifies as support work. Conversely, if it is carried out for commercial quality control, routine calibration, or general business operations, it is excluded. Similarly, if a business is conducting eligible SR&ED while simultaneously prospecting for minerals, the eligible SR&ED work may be claimed, but all work with respect to prospecting for minerals must be excluded under paragraph 248(1)(h).
Section 2: Federal ITC Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Formulas, Refundability, and Carryover Rules
2.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Rates
Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), the federal SR&ED ITC is earned at two statutory rates:

items: Basic ITC Rate (15%): Earned on 15% of the excess of a claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over total super-allowance benefit amounts. The 15% basic rate applies to corporations (other than CCPCs and ECPCs earning the enhanced rate within their expenditure limit), individuals (sole proprietorships), members of a partnership (partners), and beneficiaries of trusts. Expenditures of a CCPC or ECPC that exceed its annual expenditure limit also revert to the 15% basic rate. (Prior to 2014, the basic ITC rate was 20%.)

Enhanced ITC Rate (35%): Consists of the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.1). For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) could earn the 35% enhanced rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn the 35% enhanced rate up to their expenditure limit.

body.text: 2.2 The Annual Expenditure Limit ($3,000,000 vs. $6,000,000) and Phase-Out Rules

The maximum threshold of qualified SR&ED expenditures on which a CCPC or ECPC can earn the 35% enhanced ITC in a taxation year is governed by the corporation's expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2):

items: Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024: The maximum annual expenditure limit is $3,000,000 (available to CCPCs only, generating up to $1,050,000 of enhanced ITCs).

Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024: Following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (which had initially proposed a $4,500,000 limit), Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3) increased the maximum annual expenditure limit to $6,000,000 for both CCPCs and ECPCs (generating up to $2,100,000 of enhanced ITCs).

body.text: A. Taxable Capital Phase-Out Rules for CCPCs

For a CCPC, the annual expenditure limit decreases gradually based on the taxable capital employed in Canada (as defined in the ITA; see archived Interpretation Bulletin IT-532, Part I.3 – Tax on Large Corporations) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the immediately preceding taxation year:

items: For Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024: The $3,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease once the previous year's taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $10,000,000, and becomes nil when the previous year's taxable capital reaches $50,000,000.

For Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024: The $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease once the previous year's taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil when the previous year's taxable capital reaches $75,000,000.

body.text: If a CCPC is associated with one or more other CCPCs, the expenditure limit is calculated using the combined taxable capital of all CCPCs in the associated group and must be allocated among the associated group members under subsection 127(10.3). Short taxation years also affect the calculation of the expenditure limit, and specific rules apply where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC.
B. Revenue-Based Phase-Out Rules for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and Elective CCPC Option

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) (defined in subsection 127(9)) are eligible for the $6,000,000 expenditure limit. For an ECPC, the reduction of the expenditure limit is calculated using the average annual revenue of the preceding 3 fiscal years. If the ECPC is part of a consolidated group that prepares consolidated financial statements (presenting the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members as a single economic entity), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is shared among the members of the consolidated group, and the annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements is used to calculate the 3-year average annual revenue and expenditure limit (even if an entity leaves or joins the group during the year).

Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs may elect using the prescribed form to calculate their expenditure limit using the same 3-year average annual revenue method as ECPCs. When a CCPC makes this election, the calculation requires using the total of all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each corporation that is a member of the associated group for the taxation year in question over the preceding 3 fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout the entirety of that 3-year period.
2.3 Refundability Rules (100% vs. 40% vs. 0%) and the Qualifying Income Limit

Cash refundability of unused SR&ED ITCs is governed by section 127.1 of the ITA (specifically subsections 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01), and 127.1(3)). Before any cash refund can be issued, earned ITCs must first be applied against the taxpayer's Part I federal income tax payable for the current year. The refundability percentage applied to the unclaimed balance of current-year ITCs depends on the claimant's tax classification, whether the expenditures are within or over the expenditure limit, and whether the expenditures are current (including the PPA) or capital.
The "Qualifying Corporation", "Qualifying Income Limit", and "Excluded Corporation" Definitions (Subsection 127.1(2))
Under subsection 127.1(2) and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and SR&ED Glossary, CCPCs are divided into three categories for refundability purposes:

items: Qualifying Corporation: A corporation that is a CCPC throughout the taxation year (and is not an "excluded corporation") whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation years ending in the preceding calendar year) does not exceed the corporation's Qualifying Income Limit.

For Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000] where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount is ≤$10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which the taxable capital amount exceeds $10,000,000.

For Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000] where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount is ≤$15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which the taxable capital amount exceeds $15,000,000.

Excluded Corporation: A CCPC that is an excluded corporation under subsection 127.1(2), whose refundability is restricted to 40% across all current and capital expenditures whether under or over the expenditure limit.

CCPCs Other Than Qualifying or Excluded Corporations: A CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit (and that is not an excluded corporation) still receives a 100% refund on current expenditures and PPA up to its expenditure limit and a 40% refund on capital expenditures up to its expenditure limit, but receives 0% refundability (non-refundable) on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit.

body.text: 2.4 Carryback (3 Years), Carryforward (20 Years), and Acquisition of Control Rules

Unused SR&ED ITCs that are not deducted against current-year Part I tax payable or refunded in cash under section 127.1 are subject to the following carryover rules under subsection 127(5) and 127(9):

items: Carryback (3 Years): Unused current-year ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years. The carryback amount is limited to the lesser of (1) the current-year ITC available in excess of the amount needed to reduce current-year Part I tax to nil, and (2) the amount by which Part I tax payable in the previous year exceeds the ITC available in that previous year.
Carryforward (20 Years): Unused ITCs may be carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce future Part I tax payable.

Deemed Deduction of Applied/Refunded ITCs (Subsection 127.1(3)): Any ITC applied against Part I tax or received as a cash refund is deemed deducted and removed from the total ITCs available for carryforward or carryback. (Note that under Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. The Queen, 98-1052(IT)G, 2001, because subsection 127(5) states that a taxpayer "may" deduct credits, the taxpayer can elect the ordering of credit utilization.)

Acquisition of Control Restrictions: An acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of unused ITCs earned prior to the acquisition and restricts the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition.

body.text: Section 3: Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Proxy vs. Traditional Overhead Methods, and Cost Rules
3.1 The Closed-Category Rule and Prescribed Exclusions (Regulation 2902)

Under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA, the categories of allowable and qualified SR&ED expenditures are strictly closed. A real, documented cost plainly incurred for an eligible R&D project still earns zero tax credit unless it falls within one of the statutory expenditure categories:

items: Salary or wages of employees;
Materials consumed or Materials transformed;
Contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant;
Third-party payments to approved or qualifying entities;
Overhead and other expenditures (under the Traditional Method only) OR the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (under the Proxy Method, for ITC calculation only); and
Capital expenditures for depreciable property, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

body.text: Furthermore, Paragraph 2902(a) and Paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations designate specific "prescribed expenditures" that are excluded from ever qualifying for an ITC. Under the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (updated May 22, 2026), these prescribed exclusions include:

items: General administration or management expenses, including administrative salaries or wages and related benefits for persons whose duties are not all or substantially all (≥90%) directed to SR&ED;
Legal or accounting fees;
Interest and financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g) of the ITA;
Entertainment expenses;
Advertising or selling expenses;
Conference or convention expenses;
Dues or membership fees for scientific or technical societies;
Fines or penalties;
Costs for the maintenance and upkeep of premises, facilities, or equipment not attributable to SR&ED; and
Professional fees paid for preparing the financial or technical portions of SR&ED claims.

body.text: 3.2 Category 1: Salary or Wages (Subsections 37(1), 37(1.4), 37(9), 78(4), and Regulation 2900)

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (including fees received for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business), which generally corresponds to gross employment wages reported on a T4 slip. (As illustrated in Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 CCI 183, remuneration satisfying the subsection 248(1) definition of employment salary or wages qualifies when not excluded commission; conversely, in 2026 TCC 181, shareholder-employees paid salaries reported on T4 slips could not retroactively reclassify those amounts as dividends.)
A. Directly Engaged (Proxy Method) vs. Undertakes, Supervises, or Supports (Traditional Method)

Under the Proxy Method, only the portion of salary or wages of employees "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada may be included. "Directly engaged" applies strictly to hands-on work included in the core definition of SR&ED (basic research, applied research, or experimental development), eligible support work directly in support of it, and first-line technical supervision where managers or supervisors with relevant scientific or technological qualifications are directly conducting work, directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED, or providing direct technical input (including technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year, such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, and determining the quality of materials used). Non-technological management functions, supervision beyond the first-line level, and clerical or administrative staff (such as receptionists, secretarial staff, payroll, accounting, and legal support) are excluded under the Proxy Method.

Under the Traditional Method (Paragraph 2900(2)(b) and Paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations), claimants may include the salary or wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the prosecution of SR&ED, as well as administrative or clerical salary or wages (claimed as overhead on Line 360 of Form T661) if those administrative wages are directly attributable—meaning both directly related and incremental—to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under both methods, tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine) qualify only if the work is directly in support of and an integral part of the SR&ED and is supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications.
B. The "All or Substantially All" (ASA / 90%+) Rule and Labour Allocation

When an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA)—interpreted by the CRA as 90% or more—of their working time on eligible SR&ED duties in Canada, 100% of that employee's eligible salary or wages for the year can be included as an SR&ED expenditure. If an employee spends less than 90% of their time on SR&ED, only the actual proportion of salary or wages that can reasonably be considered to relate directly to SR&ED tasks can be claimed (Synchrosat Ltd. v. The Queen, 2000-1378(IT)I; Ergorecherche), supported by development plans, supervisor summaries, time sheets, and natural project documentation.
C. Specified Employees: Dual YMPE Caps, Bonus Prohibitions, and Form T1174

Under subsection 248(1), a "specified employee" of a corporation is an employee who is a "specified shareholder"—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation (including shares owned by any person with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length, such as a spouse, brother, or sister)—or who otherwise does not deal at arm's length with the employer.
Three strict statutory limitations apply to every specified employee:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9) and Regulation 2900(9)): Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee cannot be included in SR&ED salary or wages or in the PPA salary base.

Deductible / Direct Qualified Salary Cap (5 × YMPE): The maximum total salary or wages of a specified employee that can be claimed or deducted as an eligible SR&ED expenditure is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (Lesser of 75% and 2.5 × YMPE, Regulation 2900(7) and 2900(8)): Under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations, the portion of a specified employee's salary or wages included in the SR&ED salary base for calculating the 55% PPA is capped at the lesser of (1) 75% of the actual eligible salary or wages paid to the specified employee (for time spent on SR&ED) and (2) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year.

However, the SR&ED specified employee caps are anchored to the first earnings ceiling—the YMPE—not the YAMPE.)

Each associated corporation must file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) no later than the corporations' respective SR&ED reporting deadlines for the particular taxation years; otherwise, the amount for the salary or wages of the specified employee is deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED.
D. Bonuses, Stock Option Benefits, Taxable Benefits, and Related Benefits

For employees other than specified employees, bonuses (recognized in the taxation year the legal obligation arises for enforceable bonuses) and remuneration based on profits are allowable in direct SR&ED salary or wages, but are excluded from the PPA salary base under subsection 2900(9) and paragraphs 2900(9)(c) and (d) of the Income Tax Regulations (unless an employee's only remuneration during the year consisted of bonuses or profit-based pay for performing SR&ED duties, in which case a reasonable amount commensurate with performance is allowable). Inducements and non-competition payments are also generally considered remuneration for services rendered during employment.

Stock option benefits (under section 7 of the ITA) are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages under paragraphs 143.3(3)(a) and (b) and subsection 143.3(5) of the ITA (enacted for taxation years after November 14, 2005, overriding Alcatel, 2005 TCC 149) because they are not an actual cash outlay or expenditure incurred by the employer. Taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA are excluded from the PPA salary base, though cash outlays for taxable benefits may be included in direct SR&ED salary or wages, and non-cash taxable benefits may be included in direct SR&ED salary or wages only if (1) the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs incurred, (2) GST/HST and PST are excluded (unless no input tax credit/refund can be claimed), and (3) the actual costs (including CCA) related to the benefit are not claimed as business expenses under section 9. Conversely, the employer's share of related benefits (such as CPP/CPP2, EI, Workplace Safety and Insurance Board [WSIB], or Commission des normes, de l'équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail [CNESST]), extended vacation or sick leave, and retiring allowances (including accrued vacation/sick leave paid upon retirement) are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages (though related benefits and retiring allowances may be considered overhead under the Traditional Method).
E. Permissible Salary or Wages Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5))

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA (introduced following LGL Ltd. v. The Queen, 96-4726(IT)G), salary or wages paid to employees carrying on SR&ED work physically outside Canada may be included in the Section 37 pool if three statutory conditions are met:

items: The SR&ED work carried on outside Canada is solely in support of SR&ED work performed in Canada;
The work is performed directly by employees of the claimant who are Canadian residents; and
The salary or wages paid are not subject to income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: The total amount of permissible foreign salary or wages allowable in a taxation year is capped at "Amount B"—equal to 10% of the total allowable SR&ED salary or wages incurred for work performed inside Canada by employees during that taxation year.
F. The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4)) vs. Unpaid Current Expenditures (Subsection 127(26))
Two distinct 180-day payment rules apply to accrued SR&ED expenses:

items: Unpaid Salary or Wages (Subsection 78(4)): Any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year are treated as not having been incurred in the year for SR&ED purposes and cannot be claimed in that taxation year. Instead, the unpaid salary or wage expenditure can only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which the amount is actually paid (e.g., on Line 315 of Form T661).

Other Unpaid Current Expenditures (Subsection 127(26)): Current expenditures other than salary or wages (such as arm's-length contract invoices or material costs) incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days of the taxation year-end are deducted when calculating total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes for that year. Under subsection 127(26) and paragraph 127(9)(m), unpaid amounts must be identified on Form T661 on or before the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the taxation year in which they were incurred; if not identified by that deadline, they can never be included in calculating qualified SR&ED expenditures, even when paid in a subsequent year. For unpaid arm's-length SR&ED contracts, the claimant first reduces the contract expenditure by 20% (to 80%), deducts the unpaid portion of that 80% for the current year, and then adds 80% of the identified amount in the subsequent year when paid.

body.text: 3.3 Category 2: Overhead and Other Expenditures — Proxy Method (PPA) vs. Traditional Method
Every claimant must choose between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method for computing SR&ED expenditures on Form T661.
A. The Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(4) and 2900(6))

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, actual SR&ED overhead and other indirect expenditures cannot be included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool or in qualified SR&ED expenditures (instead, actual overhead expenses remain deductible as ordinary business expenses in computing net income). In place of actual overhead, the claimant calculates a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661.

items: The 55% Statutory Rate (Regulation 2900(4)): Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is calculated as 55% of the claimant's salary base. (The rate was 65% up to 2012, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% since 2014; claiming 65% overstates the proxy by 10 percentage points.)

Tax Treatment of the PPA: The PPA is a notional amount used only in calculating qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn the Section 127 ITC. It is not included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and cannot be deducted in computing income for tax purposes.

Overall Cap on the PPA (Regulation 2900(6)): Under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations, the calculated PPA is subject to an Overall Cap (which generally does not restrict the PPA so long as the claimant has deducted more than $55 of qualifying non-SR&ED business expenses for each $100 of eligible salary in the salary base): Overall Cap = A − B − C where:
A is the total of all amounts deducted in calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold);

B is the total of deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance, interest, bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents or brokers), Section 37 (SR&ED pool deduction per Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts); and
C is the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building.

body.text: B. The Traditional Method (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c) & 2900(3))

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated. Instead, the claimant identifies, tracks, and allocates actual overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Under paragraph 2900(2)(c) (expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED) and subsection 2900(3) / paragraph 2900(3)(a) (expenditures directly attributable to the provision, maintenance, and upkeep of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED), an overhead expenditure (or a reasonable portion thereof) qualifies only if it satisfies two mandatory tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada without an intervening step or intermediary, showing a direct causal connection to (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

body.text: C. Cloud Computing and Software Subscriptions

Because expenditure categories are closed, a cloud simulation subscription or a computer-aided design (CAD) software licence is not a qualified expenditure as a material or subcontract, however exclusively it was used for the research. Furthermore, if the claimant elects the Proxy Method, claiming cloud or software subscriptions separately is doubly barred because overhead of every kind is already represented by the 55% PPA under Regulation 2900(4). Only under the Traditional Method can directly related and incremental computing/software overhead costs (or eligible post-December 15, 2024 computer hardware/software leases and capital acquisitions) be claimed.
3.4 Category 3: Materials for SR&ED, Asset Development, and Production Runs

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.
A. Physical Tangibility, Timing, and Laid-Down Cost Rules

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" refers to all raw materials, substances, or other items that compose the body of a thing at a given moment in the overall SR&ED process. Both the materials and the "thing" (whether an intermediate product, by-product, or final product) must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state). Animals and growing things (plants) used in testing—along with associated feed, fertilizer, pesticides, herbicides, or fungicides—qualify as materials if SR&ED is performed directly on them, excluding control groups in commercial production.

items: Timing of Claim: The cost of a material can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—never at the time it is purchased, received from a supplier, or removed from inventory.

Cost Determination and Non-Arm's-Length Purchases (Subsection 127(11.6)): The allowable cost is the laid-down cost under GAAP (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition, and storage costs; or for internally manufactured inventory, raw materials, direct labour, and properly chargeable production overhead under both the Traditional and Proxy methods). Under subsection 127(11.6), if materials are purchased from a non-arm's-length party, the ITC earned is restricted to the actual cost incurred by the non-arm's-length supplier, excluding any inter-company profit markup.

body.text: B. Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

items: Materials Consumed: Materials are consumed when they are destroyed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED work. Materials remaining in inventory, forming part of a commercial asset, or forming part of experimental production sold for more than 10% of the original cost are not materials consumed.

Materials Transformed: Materials are transformed when they are converted or incorporated into another product or asset as a direct result of eligible SR&ED work and retain value (more than 10% of original cost) after the SR&ED work. Subsequent sale or conversion to commercial use of transformed materials triggers ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36).

body.text: C. Asset Development (Prototypes, Pilot Plants, Custom Assets) and Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP)
Under the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, four asset categories and two production contexts govern cost eligibility:

items: Prototypes: An original trial model or preliminary version developed to test the feasibility of a concept or hypothesis that generally has no lasting value. Duplicate copies of a prototype qualify as SR&ED materials only if built for testing directly in support of SR&ED prior to commercial production (and their costs are claimed only when testing is completed, not when built); duplicate copies built to establish inventory or meet commercial demand are excluded commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i).

Pilot Plants vs. Commercial Plants: A pilot plant is a non-commercial-scale facility isolated from normal business operations and used solely for SR&ED throughout its entire useful life. If a facility is intended for temporary or permanent conversion to commercial operations during or after SR&ED, it does not meet the definition of a pilot plant and is treated as a commercial plant, requiring strict segregation of SR&ED work from commercial work.

Experimental Production (ED+EP) vs. Simultaneous Commercial Production (ED+CP): When SR&ED is carried out simultaneously with commercial production in a manufacturing facility (ED+CP), normal commercial production costs are excluded; only incremental costs—incremental labour, incremental materials beyond normal commercial requirements, and incremental material scrap loss (actual material loss minus standard processing loss)—are allowable. Any production beyond the duration required to evaluate or validate the SR&ED is excess production and is disallowed. Conversely, proceeds from the sale of experimental production do not reduce allowable SR&ED expenditures (Les Cultures Laflamme), though transformed materials are subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial conversion (Consoltex).

CRA Administrative "Alternative Approach" and Subsection 169(2.2) Waiver: For custom commercial assets or ED+CP runs where isolating SR&ED costs from commercial costs is impossible for both the claimant and the CRA, and the CRA agrees the method is appropriate, the claimant may use the administrative estimation formula—provided the claimant signs a formal waiver of the right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the ITA: Allowable SR&ED expenditures = (total actual costs of developing the custom product or commercial asset − estimated costs that would usually be associated with constructing the asset if the technology had already existed) + estimated costs of materials transformed in SR&ED.

body.text: 3.5 Category 4: Contract Expenditures and Third-Party Payments (80% Inclusion Rule)
A. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and Paragraph 127(9)(f))

Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, when a claimant pays an arm's-length taxable Canadian supplier to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf:

items: 100% of the eligible SR&ED portion of the contract is deductible in the Section 37 pool; and
Only 80% of the arm's-length contract expenditure is included as a qualified SR&ED expenditure for calculating the Section 127 ITC (paragraph 127(9)(f)).

Contracts for Support Work Only: If a payer contracts out only support work (under paragraph 248(1)(d)) to an arm's-length contractor, the payer can claim the contract expenditure provided the support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core SR&ED performed in Canada by or on behalf of the payer. The arm's-length performer cannot claim SR&ED credits for performing support work alone.

body.text: B. Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts (Subsections 127(13) and 127(24), Form T1146)

When a claimant subcontracts SR&ED to a non-arm's-length (NAL) party (as defined in section 251 of the ITA), the contract expenditure is allowable in the payer's Section 37 deductible pool, but is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures (including support work), and the contract payment received from the NAL payer does not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures. Under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and NAL payer can jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount, reported by the performer on Line 540 of Form T661) to the payer. Under subsection 127(24), an anti-avoidance rule prevents circumventing the NAL exclusion by inserting an arm's-length intermediary between the payer and the NAL performer.
C. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii))

Under the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, a third-party payment is a payment made to a qualifying entity ("A" through "F" entities: corporations resident in Canada, approved associations, automatically approved universities and affiliated colleges, Minister-approved colleges and research institutes, tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j), and approved granting councils) to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Only 80% of a third-party payment is included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes.

body.text: 3.6 Category 5: Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Following their elimination after December 31, 2013, capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs have been restored by Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) for property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) & (B)(III))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), capital expenditures for property acquired after December 15, 2024 qualify (claimed on Line 390 and Box 782 of Form T661, with the 10 most expensive properties listed on Lines 262 and 263) if they meet the following rules:

items: Depreciable Property Available for Use After December 15, 2024: The expenditure must result in the acquisition of depreciable property (subsection 13(21)) that becomes available for use (subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024—at the earliest of when first used by the claimant to earn income (including SR&ED) or when delivered and capable of producing a commercially saleable product or service. Used equipment (entered on Line 390) and significant refurbishments made after December 15, 2024 qualify for the deduction pool, and vendor refurbishments bringing used equipment to a "new state" equal in useful life to new equipment may qualify for the ITC.

All or Substantially All (ASA / 90%+) Intention Test: At the time of acquisition, the property must be intended either (a) to be used during all or substantially all (≥90%) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (anticipated non-SR&ED operating time ≤10%), or (b) to have all or substantially all (≥90%) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.
Specific Exclusions (Paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e)): Land, buildings, leasehold interests in land or buildings, inventory, and eligible capital property (goodwill) are strictly excluded.

Interaction with CCA Schedule 8: Because an SR&ED capital expenditure deduction operates as a deemed CCA deduction, any capital expenditure claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance).

body.text: B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(11))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that fails the ≥90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial production cannot be included in the Section 37 deductible pool (it is depreciated under regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8), but qualifies for an ITC on Line 504 (and Box 792) of Form T661 if:

items: It is new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (not previously used or rented for any purpose), is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the Regulations (such as commercial plant assembly/commissioning property under paragraph 2900(11)(c)); and
Based on actual operating time, the equipment is used primarily (more than 50%, up to <90%) for SR&ED in Canada during:

First Period (First-Term SUE): From acquisition (when available for use) to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition, earning an ITC on 25% (1/4) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money under section 21 and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6)); and

Second Period (Second-Term SUE): From acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition (provided it qualified as First-Term SUE), earning an ITC on a second 25% (1/4) of the capital cost.

body.text: C. Equipment Lease Expenditures Incurred After December 15, 2024

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment acquired/leased after December 15, 2024 qualify as follows (based on actual operating time; for taxation years straddling December 16, 2024, operating time is measured after December 15, 2024):

items: Under the Proxy Method: If leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)). If used more than 50% but less than 90% ("Primarily") of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)). If used 50% or less, 0% is claimable. GPOEF (furniture, desks, chairs, photocopiers, telephones, cell phones, calculators) is excluded under the Proxy Method, but computers (including hardware, software, and ancillary equipment) are NOT considered GPOEF and therefore qualify.

Under the Traditional Method: If leased equipment (including GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) in SR&ED, 100% is claimable as a lease cost (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)). If used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED, the proportional SR&ED percentage may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c)).

Building Leases (Subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i)): Rent for a building is strictly disallowed, except for lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance Canada under Section 2903 of the Regulations.

body.text: 3.7 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, recapture of an SR&ED ITC is triggered (and added to Part I tax payable) when four conditions are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property (materials transformed, ASA capital property, or SUE) in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (subsection 127(36) lookback); (2) the cost was a qualified expenditure; (3) an ITC was earned on that cost; and (4) in the current year, the claimant disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use (for SUE, conversion occurs only when SR&ED use becomes merely incidental).

The recapture amount under subsection 127(27) is the lesser of (1) the ITC actually earned on the particular property and (2) the applicable ITC percentage applied to the proceeds of disposition (arm's-length sale) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property (conversion to commercial use or NAL disposition). Recapture does not apply to salaries, wages, or overhead, to IP sales, to NAL transfers where the property continues to be used ASA for SR&ED by the transferee (subsections 127(13), 127(29), 127(33)–(35)), or where scrap proceeds or FMV are less than 10% of the total cost of the property.
Section 4: Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Stacking Arithmetic
4.1 Statutory Reduction Rules: Paragraphs 12(1)(x), 37(1)(d), and Subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), and 127(18)

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) (for the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool) and subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18) (for Section 127 qualified SR&ED expenditures), claims are reduced dollar-for-dollar by all amounts of government assistance, non-government assistance, and (under subsection 127(18)) contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED:

items: Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9)): Assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including a Crown corporation, foreign government, provincial/territorial R&D tax credit, or indirect assistance through a government-funded non-profit organization) whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance, other than the federal SR&ED ITC.

Non-Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9) and Paragraph 12(1)(x)): An amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)) as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance.

Project-by-Project Reduction and Form T1145: Under subsection 127(18), assistance and contract payments reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures strictly on a project-by-project basis up to the total project costs for that year, with any excess carried forward to reduce future qualified expenditures on that same project (or allocated among non-arm's-length group members performing SR&ED on that project using prescribed Form T1145 under subsection 127(20)).

body.text: 4.2 Treatment of Provincial Tax Credits Attributable to the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)
Under Section 4.5 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy:

items: Reduction of Qualified Expenditures (Subsection 127(18)): Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits reduce federal qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year earned under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, including the portion of the provincial credit earned on the notional 55% PPA.

Exclusion from Section 37 Pool Grind and Inclusion Under Paragraph 12(1)(x): Because the PPA is a notional amount that is not included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit attributable to the PPA (as well as the portion of a Québec R&D credit earned on support salaries that do not qualify under the federal Proxy Method) does not reduce the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d); instead, it must be included directly in business income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the taxation year in which it is received.

body.text: 4.3 Contract Payments vs. Fixed-Price Commercial Contracts (Com Dev Ltd.)

Where a client pays a performer to carry out SR&ED on the client's behalf, subsection 127(18) reduces the performer's qualified expenditure pool by the contract payment. However, as established in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (96-4343(IT)G, 1999), a commercial fixed-price contract to deliver a finished product where the vendor bears the financial and technical risk is not a "contract payment" for the purchase of SR&ED, preserving the performer's ITC entitlement.
Section 5: Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Deadlines, Compliance, and Audit Process
5.1 Governing Bodies and Prescribed Forms

The federal SR&ED program is legislated through the Department of Finance Canada and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Within the CRA's 10 Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs), claims selected for review are evaluated by two specialists: a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager, RTM), who evaluates whether the R&D work meets subsection 248(1) eligibility requirements, and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager, FRM), who audits the claimed expenditures and ITC calculations.
To claim SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must file the following prescribed forms containing the prescribed information:

items: Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim): Mandatory for all claimants, comprising Part 1 (General information), Part 2 (Project technical descriptions and evidence items on Lines 270–282, plus top 10 post-Dec 15, 2024 capital properties on Lines 262–263), Part 3 (Allowable SR&ED expenditures and Section 37 deductible pool, including Line 315 for paid prior-year unpaid wages, Line 360 for Traditional overhead, Line 390 for capital expenditures, and Line 440 for CCA recapture), Part 4 (Qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes, including Line 504 for SUE and Line 535/540 for transferred expenditures), Part 5 (Calculation of the 55% PPA), Part 6 (Project-by-project costs), Part 7 (Additional information), Part 8 (Claim checklist), Part 9 (Claim preparer information), and Part 10 (Certification).
Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporations, or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for individuals and trusts.
Form T5013 (Partnership Information Return) for partnerships under Regulation 229 (where Form T661 is filed at the partnership level and credits flow to partners under subsection 127(8)).

body.text: 5.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline (Subsections 37(11), 37(12), 127(9)(m), and 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. For corporations, because the T2 return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of the taxation year, the SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year.

Under subsection 220(2.2) (enacted after Alex Parallel Computers, T-1512-97), the Minister has no statutory authority or discretion to extend the 18-month reporting deadline for prescribed SR&ED forms. Under subsection 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m), if Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing all prescribed information are not filed on or before the 18-month deadline (as illustrated in Easyway Cattle Co., 2015 TCC 211, and Westsource, 2017 TCC 9), the expenditures are permanently disallowed from both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 ITC.
5.3 Pre-Claim Services, Service Standards, Audit Process, and Statutory Penalties

items: Pre-Claim Services & FTCAS: The CRA offers the interactive online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), on-demand Pre-Claim Consultations and Pre-Claim Reviews (Pre-Claim Approval), and the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) for first-time claimants or those who have not claimed in 3 years (which is an educational advisory meeting, not an audit).

Official CRA Processing Service Standards (Refundable Claims Only): 60 calendar days for complete claims accepted as filed; 90 calendar days for claims selected for expenditure-only review where all projects received Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for full review. (Non-refundable claims have no service standard.)

Review Procedure & Dispute Resolution: Once selected for review, an SR&ED claim cannot be withdrawn. Reviews are conducted predominantly via virtual videoconferencing (with on-site visits granted on an exceptional case-by-case basis). RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating arbitrary settlement percentages. If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package (with the draft SR&ED Review Report), granting the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations. After a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 calendar days to file a formal Notice of Objection, followed by the right to appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1)–162(5.3)): If required claim preparer and billing arrangement information in Part 9 of Form T661 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty applies under subsection 162(5.1), for which the claimant and claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable (subject to the due diligence defence under subsection 162(5.2)). However, Part 9 is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline, and an error in Part 9 does not disallow the SR&ED claim.

Gross Negligence Penalties (Subsections 163(2) and 163(2.1)): Under subsection 163(2) (where the CRA bears the burden of proof under subsection 163(3)), knowingly or under gross negligence making a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim triggers a civil penalty equal to the greater of $100 and 50% of the sum of (1) the understated Part I tax payable (paragraph 163(2)(a), with taxable income in loss years deemed not less than zero under subsection 163(2.1)) plus (2) the overstated refundable ITC claimed (paragraph 163(2)(d)).

body.text: Section 6: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and 2025–2026 Harmonization Analysis

Ten Canadian jurisdictions—Québec, Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon—offer statutory corporate R&D tax credits or grants that stack with the federal SR&ED program. Because provincial and territorial R&D credits constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the federal ITA, they reduce federal qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year earned under subsection 127(18) (unless formally renounced or waived where permitted).
6.1 Québec: The New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (2025–2026 Reform)

In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget (tabled March 25, 2025), Québec abolished eight legacy R&D tax measures—including the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, and the industrial design component of the in-house design credit—for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025. In their place, Québec enacted the consolidated, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC):

items: Credit Rates and $1,000,000 Bracket: Regardless of corporate size or ownership (available to CCPCs, public corporations, and foreign subsidiaries operating an establishment in Québec), the CRIC provides a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable rate on all eligible expenditures exceeding $1,000,000 (note: corporate members of a partnership earn only the 20% base rate on their partnership share).

Modified Exclusion Threshold Formula: Qualified expenditures in a taxation year must exceed a single annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of (1) $50,000 (pro-rated for short taxation years) or (2) the sum of the individual employee exclusion thresholds, where each employee's threshold equals the Basic Personal Amount (BPA) under the Québec personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025) multiplied by the percentage of time that employee spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities: Exclusion threshold = greater of $50,000 and Σ (BPA × % of each employee's time spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities)

R&D Plus Pre-Commercialization Scope: In addition to R&D activities (harmonized with the federal definition and scientifically reviewed by the CRA, while excluding routine maintenance/evolution of internal IT systems), the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec as a continuation of Québec R&D: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements to obtain initial approval or certification for marketing an innovation; (2) product design (form, shape, aesthetics, functionality improvements, and choice of materials); and (3) implementing a quality control system strictly required for initial regulatory approval or certification.

Eligible Expenses, Capital Property Recovery, and Form RD-1029.8.CR-T: Qualified expenditures consist of 100% of eligible salaries and wages, 50% of Québec subcontractor payments (including 50% of payments to eligible Québec universities, public research centres, or research consortia), and 100% of acquisition costs for new depreciable capital equipment used ≥90% in Québec R&D or pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, and property in a large investment project; subject to a special recovery tax if the property ceases to be used solely in Québec for eligible activities within 730 consecutive days). Claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (or RD-1029.8.CR) with the Québec CO-17 return. (Separately, the 30% Québec Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business [TCEB] shifts its refundable/non-refundable split to 23%/7% in 2025, 22%/8% in 2026, 21%/9% in 2027, and 20%/10% in 2028+, and is halved to 15% total for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025 when ≥50% of IT work is outsourced outside Québec.)

body.text: 6.2 Ontario: OITC (8%), ORDTC (3.5%), and OBRITC (20%) (Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario))
Ontario administers three R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all contingent on filing a federal Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 within 18 months of fiscal year-end:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule 566, Line 468 of Schedule 5): An 8% fully refundable credit for corporations on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (maximum $240,000 refund, shared among associated corporations). Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 limit; the $3,000,000 OITC limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year specified capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. May be waived under subsection 96(14).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45, Schedule 508, Line 416 of Schedule 5): A 3.5% non-refundable credit (since June 1, 2016; previously 4.5%) with no expenditure limit, carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years (waivable under subsection 43(1); subject to 23.56% recapture under section 45 on Line 277 of Schedule 5). Because the OITC is government assistance, the OITC is calculated first and reduces the eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules 568 & 569, Line 470 of Schedule 5): A 20% fully refundable credit on qualified expenditures under eligible contracts with designated Ontario Eligible Research Institutes (universities, colleges, research hospitals, Centres of Excellence) up to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap ($4,000,000 maximum annual credit).

Capital Equipment Restoration (2026): Confirmed in Ontario's October 29, 2026 Fall Economic Statement, federal Bill C-15 restored depreciable capital equipment eligibility (acquired on or after December 16, 2024 and used ASA ≥90% in Ontario SR&ED) to Ontario's R&D credits.
