body.text: 6.4 Worked Mathematical Stacking Examples (Federal + Provincial Integration)
Because provincial R&D tax credits are classified as government assistance under subsection 127(18), they reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base before the 35% federal rate is applied:

items: Ontario CCPC Example ($1,000,000 Eligible Salaries, Proxy Method): Direct SR&ED salaries of $1,000,000 plus the 55% PPA ($550,000) generate $1,550,000 in gross qualified expenditures. First, the 8% refundable OITC on Schedule 566 yields $124,000 (8% × $1,550,000). Second, the $124,000 OITC reduces the ORDTC base to $1,426,000 ($1,550,000 - $124,000), yielding $49,910 of non-refundable ORDTC (3.5% × $1,426,000) on Schedule 508. Third, both Ontario credits reduce the federal qualified expenditure base under subsection 127(18) to $1,376,090 ($1,550,000 - $124,000 - $49,910), generating $481,631.50 in 35% refundable federal ITCs (35% × $1,376,090), for a total combined return of $655,541.50 (65.55% of salary, of which $605,631.50 or 60.56% is immediate cash—or $623,100 / 62.31% in cash if the CCPC waives the non-refundable ORDTC under subsection 43(1)).

Québec CCPC Example ($1,000,000 Eligible Salaries Across 10 Full-Time Researchers, Proxy Method): Under the CRIC, the exclusion threshold for 10 full-time R&D employees is $185,710 (10 × $18,571, exceeding the $50,000 minimum), leaving $814,290 of net qualified Québec expenditures. At the 30% CRIC rate (up to $1,000,000), the refundable Québec CRIC is $244,287.00. Deducting $244,287.00 from the $1,550,000 federal qualified expenditure base ($1,000,000 salary + $550,000 PPA) leaves $1,305,713, which earns a 35% federal refundable ITC of $456,999.55, yielding $701,286.55 (70.13% of direct salary) in total cash refunds.

body.text: Section 7: Judicial Jurisprudence, CRA Eligibility Guidelines ("Why" and "How"), and Audit Precedents (1988–2026)
7.1 The Foundational Five-Question Framework: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998)

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED law is Chief Justice Bowman's decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), which established the five mandatory questions for evaluating SR&ED eligibility under subsection 248(1) (and recognized "system uncertainty" where known components interact unpredictably):

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technical risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?

Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty (comprising five stages: (a) observing the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulating a clear objective; (c) identifying and articulating the technological uncertainty; (d) formulating a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses)?

Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?

Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement (noting that under Rainbow Pipe Line, 1999, RIS-Christie, and Canafric, the rejection or falsification of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement)?
Detailed Progressive Records: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 7.2 Appellate Endorsement and Evidentiary Jurisprudence: Sass Manufacturing, RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, and Les Abeilles

In Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363, [1988] 1 CTC 2524 (TCC), Judge Sarchuk established that "systematic investigation" requires a planned, methodical search with recorded results rather than unrecorded trial and error. Subsequently, in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 CTC 132 (FCA), Justice Robertson held that (1) third-party documentary "repeatability" is not an absolute legal precondition to claiming SR&ED; (2) proving that testing resolved an engineering problem to achieve a technological advancement raises a rebuttable inference that the testing was carried out systematically; (3) both oral (viva voce) and documentary evidence are admissible; (4) actual project success is not required; and (5) what constitutes SR&ED is a question of law or mixed law and fact for the court, not expert witnesses. In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740, the Federal Court of Appeal formally summarized and endorsed the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria.

In Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, Justice Jorré held at paragraph 94 that while lacking contemporaneous records places a taxpayer in a "very precarious position," "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific content, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development," and credible oral testimony can establish eligibility—reflecting the Supreme Court of Canada's statutory interpretation principles in 65302 British Columbia Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 804 and Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 that administrative policies cannot add unlegislated statutory conditions.
7.3 Routine Engineering, the 2021 "Why and How" Guidelines, and 2021–2026 Jurisprudence

Conversely, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355 (thermoformed plastic Multi-Bins) and Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (theatre fire-curtain hydraulic backwind and manual override), the courts confirmed that product novelty, systematic routine engineering using known methods, or subjective lack of knowledge by non-engineers without consulting standard engineering principles fails to establish objective technological uncertainty.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (decided May 10, 2021), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected the taxpayer's argument that the scientific method criterion should not apply because the words "scientific method" do not appear in subsection 248(1). After the CRA issued its August 13, 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives—condensing the analysis into the "Why" Requirement (generating conceptual knowledge to overcome a scientific or technological uncertainty) and the "How" Requirement (conducting a systematic investigation via 1. formulating a hypothesis, 2. testing by experiment or analysis, 3. developing logical conclusions, and 4. keeping progressive evidence)—the taxpayer in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 argued that the revised guidelines had rejected the Northwest Hydraulic criteria. The Federal Court of Appeal dismissed that appeal as well, holding that CRA guidance is not binding on the courts and that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the authoritative legal test.

Most recently, between 2023 and October 2026, the courts decided Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 50 (allowing six food-science projects where failed recipe iterations were systematically analysed), DAZZM Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129 (allowing cloud SaaS React/Redux integration on systemic uncertainty and confirming at para. 119 that contemporaneous timesheets are not mandatory), Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173 (holding that plagiarized supplier/website text in Form T661 narratives was a misrepresentation reopening statute-barred years), Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7 (allowing an SIL 4 train-control project on cumulative system uncertainty while disallowing $1,293,692 for a routine SCADA modernization/scale-up), and Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175 (decided October 21, 2026, aff'g 2025 TCC 183) (upholding the disallowance of 13 food-processing projects and holding that a trial judge's finding that a taxpayer's witness is "credible" does not, by itself, demolish the Minister's reassessment assumptions when the substance of the testimony describes trial-and-error rather than systematic hypothesis testing).
